To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the information content of an image is proportional to the square of the average energy of the photons incident on the detector, and is independent of the energy distribution of the photons; and (2) the information content per unit area in an image is proportional only to the number of photons absorbed in the image, and is independent both of the energy distribution and of the average energy per photon.

the information content of a radiographic image depends strongly on the spectral distribution of x-rays incident on the detecting surface and that the spectral distribution of incident x-rays depends strongly on both the voltage of the x-ray tube and the material of the anode.

the spectral distribution of x-rays has a significant effect on the information content of radiographs and that the effect can be corrected for by using a simple, easily implemented method that is applicable to any x-ray source.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development of methods for determining the information content in radiographs, and the use of this information to determine optimal operating parameters of the imaging system, and to develop techniques for obtaining images at substantially lower doses.
the development of a theoretical foundation for radiography.
developing a quantitative basis for the optimization of x-ray systems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the spectral distribution of an x-ray beam is a significant factor in determining the minimum dose required for a diagnostic radiograph, but that it can be taken into account in a simple and accurate manner.

the minimum exposure required for a given diagnostic x-ray examination is determined by the information content of the object being imaged and by the information content required for the diagnostic purpose.
the spectral distribution of an x-ray beam is a significant factor in determining the minimum exposure needed for a given information content in a diagnostic image.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a substantial increase in the information content of a diagnostic radiograph can be achieved with only a modest increase in dose.

the minimum exposure required for a specified information set is proportional to the square of the mean energy, inversely proportional to the square root of the number of photons per pixel, and inversely proportional to some power of the number of pixels.
a more complete theory of x-ray information theory can be developed, but that the simpler theory can be used to obtain results of sufficient accuracy for most applications.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the present method of recording mammograms is inefficient and that there is room for substantial improvements in the information recorded in a mammogram at a substantially lower dose than is currently used.

it should be possible to reduce the dose in radiography by a factor of two or three, without compromising diagnostic quality, by using the present computational methods to optimize the x-ray spectrum.
the spectral distribution of x-ray fluence should be taken into account in the development of methods for improving the efficiency of the use of x-ray information in medical imaging.
